spoken: [hook] Saving recipes feels like learning to cook. It isn't. || Here's why. It's Tuesday, seven in the evening, and you're tired. You open your two hundred saved recipes, scroll for twenty minutes, and end up making toast. || Do that four nights a week, and that's eighty minutes just deciding. And you're still no better at cooking than you were in January. || [turn] So here's the fix. Stop collecting. Pick three dinners you'd happily eat every week, and master just those. Say, dal, a tomato pasta, and a bean chili. || Cook each one twice this week. By the second time, you'll barely look at the recipe. || And write one shopping list for all three. They share the same base, onions, tomatoes and garlic, so nothing goes to waste. || [turn] So what does your week look like by Sunday? || [land] Three recipes. Six home dinners. And zero minutes standing at the fridge, wondering what to make. || Here's the rule. Pick three. Cook each one twice. One list. Send this to the friend with three hundred saved recipes. || [outro] That's what Dmyor is for. You archive your dream today, so you can see it tomorrow, and break it down into small steps you can actually do. || [outro] And follow, because this afternoon's reel is how twenty minutes a day turned into a wedding gift. || [outro] If you want to try it out, I've put the link in the bio.

params.title: How 20 minutes a day became a wedding gift

caption.instagram:
Saving recipes feels like learning to cook. It isn't.

200 saved, 20 minutes scrolling, toast again. Four nights a week that's 80 minutes just deciding.

The 3-recipe rule:
1. Pick 3 dinners you'd happily eat every week (dal, tomato pasta, bean chili)
2. Cook each one twice this week
3. One shopping list for all three: they share onions, tomatoes, garlic

By Sunday: 6 home dinners, 0 minutes at the fridge wondering what to make.

Send this to the friend with 300 saved recipes.
